George Grenville's ministry proposed the Stamp Act in Britain's postwar revenue program.
The 1773 Tea Act changed tea trade privileges to help the financially troubled Company; the existing colonial tea duty was not repealed.
Boston protest organizers objected to shipments of East India Company tea and some participants destroyed the cargo.
The royal governor opposed protesters' demands to return tea ships without fulfilling customs obligations.
First Continental Congress organized colonial objections to parliamentary acts and coordinated a boycott in 1774.
Pontiac helped organize Indigenous resistance to British military posts in the Great Lakes region after the war; this does not make all Indigenous nations one political organization.
Western land investors opposed or sought changes to British policies restricting settlement and territorial claims.
Thomas Hutchinson Jr. was the colonial governor's son; a family connection is not evidence of control over appointment.
Elisha Hutchinson was the colonial governor's son; the son's prospective commission is not proof the father received it.
Named Boston consignee expected to receive tea and a reported 6% commission on sales if completed; not proof of actual payment.
Named Boston consignee expected to receive tea and a reported 6% commission on sales if completed; not proof of actual payment.
Richard Clarke was associated with mercantile firm Richard Clarke & Sons in Boston.
Company designated the Clarke family's business to receive tea in Boston.
Joshua Winslow wrote directly about his appointment as a Company agent and expected commission.
Benjamin Faneuil Jr. was a tea consignee in the merchant partnership with Joshua Winslow.
Commonwealth Museum identifies Brook Watson as a London merchant who recommended Joshua Winslow.
Commonwealth Museum identifies Brook Watson as recommending Benjamin Faneuil Jr. and business partner Winslow.
Contemporary research edition identifies these men as partners in a Boston tea-consignee firm.
November 18 1773 letter from Winslow to Gay describes the tea appointment and prospect of commission.
Bank of England archive records a note about prolonging an existing £50,000 Company loan; not evidence of a fresh £50,000 disbursement.
The 1766 banking archive identifies Henry Crabb Boulton as East India Company chairman/director.
Burgoyne chaired a parliamentary committee whose inquiries led to May 1773 debate on Clive's administration in India.
After Company financial crisis, Parliament enacted 1773 legislation enabling lending; an 1813 account discusses £1.4 million.
Lord North was prime minister when government undertook 1773 financial and regulatory responses to the Company's crisis.
William III, with Mary II, granted the 1694 charter to a new bank designed to fund government war borrowing.
Mary II and William III were among original Bank stockholders; archive details a combined royal £10,000 Bank-stock investment.
William III and Mary II invested in original Bank stock according to first stock ledger.
John Houblon was appointed the Bank's first governor.
The Bank's founding £1.2m capital financed a government loan at 8% interest, secured by specified taxation.
1661 charter expanded the Company's authority to govern settlements and maintain armed forces.
British Library records £324,150 in aggregate loans from old East India Company to monarch between 1660–1684; this edge covers a period and is not dated as one transfer.
Chancellor Charles Montagu prepared a 1698 £2m public-borrowing scheme offering trade privileges to subscribers.
Most of the public-debt subscribers were incorporated as a joint-stock East India trading company.
The old East India Company held £315,000 of stock in the rival English Company via treasurer John Du Bois. Record is a stake, not evidence of a new 1698 cash transfer.
Competing East India companies' stocks and trading were united, with the old company's charter surrendered by 1709.
South Sea Company issued stock in exchange for government debts as part of the early eighteenth-century debt restructuring system.
Contemporary bank archive catalogue identifies competing proposals to Parliament in 1719–1720.
A Bank archival agreement dated October 23 1722 concerns buying South Sea stock; execution and exact cash transfers require ledger records.

Mays and Shea's 2011 ledger comparison estimates approximately 700 account owners in both institutions in 1719 and 760 by 1721. These are aggregate accounts, not proof of centrally coordinated investors, related families, or verified distinct persons.
East India Company directors appointed representatives to meet Bank and South Sea Company representatives in September 1720 amid a credit crisis.
East India Company representatives considered proposals to help manage South Sea debts after the collapse, but did not carry out the proposed 1721 engraftment.
Walpole proposed redistributing South Sea capital across major financial companies; an authorizing act followed in 1721 but the contemplated engraftment did not take place.
Weavers and manufacturing interests sought legislation restricting imports and use of Indian cotton calicoes, with petitions and protests differing by locality.
A June 1721 law restricted foreign-routed East India goods into British colonies, strengthening the Company's imperial commercial privileges.
Bank archival director lists name Michael Godfrey the first Deputy Governor in July 1694.
Bank archives name Henry Furnese among the first directors in 1694. This does not establish any holdings in rival companies.
John Law created Banque Générale in 1716 with regency permission to issue paper notes.
Law's private banking enterprise shifted into royal control during 1718–1719; different historical summaries vary in transition details, so no exact day is asserted.
The French regent backed Law's bank and trading privileges as part of postwar fiscal reform.
John Law created Compagnie d'Occident in 1717 to pursue Louisiana commerce and French public-debt restructuring.
French regency authorities entrusted Louisiana trading monopoly rights to the Compagnie d'Occident in 1717.
The Company of the West and other French overseas commercial interests were grouped into the Compagnie des Indes by May 1719.
The French Company was used to issue shares against public debt and gained quasi-governmental monetary and fiscal privileges.
John Law became Controller General of Finances in January 1720 during the French debt-conversion experiment.
Company settlement and Louisiana resource claims affected many distinct Indigenous communities. This umbrella population label is not evidence that the communities acted with one unified voice.
French Company colonial projects involved plantations and labor extracted from enslaved Africans; documenting this harm is not an ownership claim over free agents.
BnF historian Cécile Vidal describes Bienville selecting the New Orleans site with assistance from Indigenous advisors; individual advisers are not identified in this account.
Historical Federal Reserve commentary identifies John Blunt as South Sea Company director, but does not establish Law and Blunt personally coordinated.
Quinn and Turner argue South Sea directors followed Law's example in proposing broad government debt conversion. This is scholarly interpretation of influence, not a claim of joint management.
Antoine Crozat held earlier Louisiana commercial privileges before the 1717 Law company's charter; no transfer fee or personal investment is inferred.
Hutcheson's 1720 public pamphlet contests the published value calculations for South Sea shares; full numerical analysis not yet transcribed.
The April 20 order restricted large-silver coin exchange, and August 30 edict addressed inventory and destruction of specified banknotes; not a record of completed exchanges or destruction.

A French colonial official identified as Diron signed Louisiana enumerations in 1721 and wrote a related January 1722 report. This is administrative reporting, not evidence of individual people's consent.
A Paris note dated 23 Dec 1719 certifies the bearer received twenty bank-equity shares from Mr. Imbert; signatory Frenier. No cash sale price, personal profit or recipient identity is established.
Frenier signed the manuscript acknowledging the bearer received shares from Imbert. Frenier is the signatory, not necessarily the share recipient or transferor, and no personal meeting is proven.
MSS606 finding aid identifies Mr. Imbert as first valet of Duke Philippe d'Orléans, creating a documented court-office connection but not proving the Regent arranged the recorded share release.

Choctaw representatives initiated a 1721 request for French trade access on Choctaw lands; Biloxi's colonial council accepted in principle but did not immediately build the facility. Exact February council meeting day is unresolved.
Continued Choctaw diplomatic requests in 1725 brought the French Superior Council to transmit the request to Company authorities amid British trade competition.
The French Council conveyed Choctaw representatives' demand for a stock of trade goods in 1725; council correspondence cites ANOM C13A vol.9 fol.65v.
Choctaw leaders met French governor Périer in 1729 to negotiate a trading establishment and the circumstances of French military protection in Choctaw territory.
Choctaw political leaders' sustained diplomatic initiative led to the Youanis post's establishment around 1730, while French officers depended on Choctaw security and local acceptance.
French officer Régis du Roullet supervised construction of the trading post at Haiyowvni/Youanis in February–March 1730.

Choctaw leaders maintained formal diplomacy and trade relations with French officials; the Choctaw Nation's historical accounts describe gifts, boundaries and community governance, not unilateral French ownership.
Diron d'Artaguiette held a colonial-authorized exclusive privilege over French trade affecting Choctaw territory in the late 1720s; this did not confer sovereignty over the Choctaw people.
Périer proceeded with a Choctaw-requested trading post despite existing Diron commercial privileges and Company reluctance about expense.
Study citing ANOM C13A 1732 fols.33–33v reports Superior Council awarded Diron 29,000 French livres for loss of exclusive trade interests; not proof of actual funds paid.
HNOC archival guide indexes a September 2 1732 ministerial letter approving the Superior Council decision involving Diron and Company of Indies, amount not specified in abstract.

Original February 9–10 1730 correspondence is catalogued as mentioning the Diron–Périer conflict over Régis du Roullet's Choctaw visit. This is not evidence that Diron or Roullet conspired financially.
Merveilleux offered a French trade post proposal involving Choctaw territory in 1726, but the proposal was not adopted. He cannot be treated as founding the eventual 1730 post.
Royal decree indexes the Company's 1731 relinquishment of administrative concession for Louisiana and Illinois back to Crown; legal articles and effective date pending direct reading.

Jan 19 1732 official report catalogued by HNOC: Salmon took possession of certain Company fortifications and other assets for king, with exceptions. An officer's report does not prove a comprehensive inventory.
BnF catalogues royal 1733 Council of State decree regulating debt payment for the Company's former Louisiana undertakings; catalog is not specific financial settlement.
Official Jan 1732 letter indexed by HNOC mentions Salmon–MacMahon disagreement about Company merchandise and brick remaining amid Crown transfer.
Sep 2 1732 ministerial letter to Salmon references approval of a Council decision involving Diron and Company; the 29,000-livre amount not mentioned by archival catalogue.

University of Limoges historical legal research cites ANOM F3 242 fol.190: royal 22 May 1731 reorganization of Superior Council excluded former Company of Indies directors; original roster and detailed articles still need verification.
